title: Do Students Benefit from Attending Better Schools? Evidence from Rule-based Student Assignments in Trinidad and Tobago
research_question: Do students experience improved academic outcomes—such as test performance, examinations passed, and qualifications for tertiary education—when they attend secondary schools that enroll higher-achieving peers? Do these benefits differ by student gender, and are the marginal returns to attending a school with marginally higher-achieving peers non-linear across the school quality distribution?
data_description: The study combines two administrative datasets from Trinidad and Tobago's Ministry of Education. The first is the 2000 Secondary Entrance Assessment (SEA) records for the entire cohort of 31,593 fifth-grade students, containing scores on five SEA subjects (mathematics, English, science, social studies, essay), the four ordered secondary school choices each student listed, gender, age, religion code, primary school district, and the secondary school assigned. The second source is the 2004 and 2005 Caribbean Secondary Examination Certification (CSEC) records, taken at the end of tenth grade, including grades on each subject and the secondary school attended. Linking by name, gender, and birthdate matched 22,876 students; the final analytic sample is 23,322 students across 98 public secondary schools. Outcomes include CSEC participation, number of exams taken and passed, English and math grades, and earning a certificate (five passes including English and math).
institutional_context: Trinidad and Tobago operates a centralized, ability-grouped secondary school system. After fifth grade, every student sits the SEA examination and submits four ranked secondary school choices. The Ministry of Education then assigns students through a sequential algorithm: the most oversubscribed school fills its slots first with its highest-scoring applicants, then the next, and so on, generating effective test-score cut-offs at each school. Higher-achieving students typically list and gain entry to more selective schools, while lower scorers are funneled into less prestigious schools. There are 123 public secondary schools across three types (Government, Government-assisted, and Comprehensive), all teaching a common national curriculum, and private schools play only a marginal role. Government-assisted schools, often elite religious institutions, are permitted to hand-pick 20% of their incoming class, while the remaining 80% and all places at other schools are filled strictly by the rule.

_legacy_v1_ground_truth.conclusion_detail: Attending a better school positively impacts students' academic performance and future educational outcomes.
